Compare Camera Specs

How we check camera and lens specs

Every spec on this site is checked against the camera or lens maker's own published figures. This page explains which sources we trust, which number we store when a maker quotes several, and how a check works. When a rule changes, the old one stays in the log at the bottom.

The short version

  • The maker decides. Its own spec page, manual or press release is enough on its own.
  • Retailers, Wikipedia, spec databases and AI summaries never set a number. They copy each other, errors included.
  • One rule per spec, for every brand. Makers quote battery life, stabilization and viewfinder size in different ways. We pick one way and convert everything to it, so a comparison is fair.
  • Sources are shown. Each item we've checked lists its sources in the References section at the bottom of the comparison.
  • No guessing. If we can't confirm a figure, we say so instead of filling the gap.

Which sources we trust

Not every source gets a vote.

SourceCan it set a spec?Why
The makerYes, aloneIts spec page for this exact mount, its regional sites (Canon Japan, Panasonic Japan…), spec PDFs, owner's manuals and press releases. Nobody knows the product better.
Reviews that measureOnly as a backupLensTip, Opticallimits, DPReview and similar weigh and measure the gear themselves. We use them only when the maker's figure is missing, unclear, covers several mounts at once, or is physically impossible.
RetailersNever for specsMost stores copy the same distributor feed, mistakes and all. We use them for prices only.
Spec databasesNeverOne we tested matched the makers' numbers but had about 30% of its mount labels wrong.
Wikipedia, rumor sites, AI summariesNeverThey are only as good as what they copy from, and they often copy each other.

When sources still disagree:

  • The maker wins. We never average two numbers.
  • A maker can disagree with itself. Canon UK lists the EOS R8 as weather-resistant; Canon Japan doesn't. Then we look for a third Canon source before changing anything, and until we find one, the cautious value stays.
  • One table for many mounts is a trap. Lens makers often print one set of figures for every mount, usually the original version's. Weight and length really do differ by mount (L-Mount barrels run about 2 mm shorter than Sony E ones), so we use the per-mount page.
  • A blocked page proves nothing. If a site refuses us, we try a browser, another regional site, then a measured review.
  • A new version is a new item. We never "correct" a lens to its Mark II's specs.

Which number we store

Makers quote the same thing in different ways. Battery life alone comes in Normal and Economy modes, with the screen or the viewfinder. These are the rules that make the numbers comparable.

Cameras

SpecWhat we storeWhy
WeightWith battery and memory cardIt's what you carry. If a maker gives only the body weight, we use its with-battery figure for the identical body.
SizeThe maker's headline width × height × depthSome makers also quote depth to the screen or grip; the headline figure is the one every maker gives.
ResolutionEffective megapixels. Sigma's Foveon sensors: the top layer onlyThe top layer sets the size of the photo; Sigma's all-layer count isn't comparable with ordinary sensors.
Viewfinder sizeFull-frame equivalent magnification. Fujifilm X100 and X-Pro: the optical finderSome makers quote a native figure that makes crop-sensor finders look bigger than they are. The optical finder is what defines the X100 and X-Pro.
StabilizationStops from the body aloneFigures with a stabilized lens attached depend on the lens, so they don't compare across bodies.
Battery lifeCIPA shots per charge, Normal mode, with the screen; a separate viewfinder figure when the maker gives oneEconomy modes inflate the number. Brand details: Nikon with energy saving off, Panasonic two-card bodies with an SD card, X100 and X-Pro with the electronic and optical finders.
BurstTop mechanical rate and top electronic rate, kept apartElectronic first curtain counts as mechanical (the rear curtain is still mechanical). Nikon's reduced-resolution capture modes don't count.
Weather sealingYes only when the maker claims itSee below.

Lenses

SpecWhat we storeWhy
WeightThe bare lens: no hood, caps or tripod footAccessories come off, and some makers include them while others don't.
LengthMount to front, zoomed out to its shortest, no hoodHoods are optional and vary in size.
DiameterThe widest part of the barrelNot the filter thread, which is often smaller.
Close focusFrom the sensor; for zooms, the closest anywhere in the range; the autofocus figure when the maker also gives a manual-focus oneAutofocus is how most people will focus. Maximum magnification follows the same rule.
ApertureWidest f-number at the wide end, never a T-stop. Smallest aperture on variable zooms: also the wide endBoth apertures are then read at the same focal length.
Equivalent focal lengthFocal length × crop: 1.5 (Fujifilm X, Sony APS-C, Nikon DX), 1.6 (Canon RF-S), 2.0 (Micro Four Thirds)So a 23mm on APS-C and a 35mm on full frame show the same framing. Dual-fisheye VR lenses take no crop.
YearFirst year on sale in this mountA lens can arrive on a new mount years after the original.
Same lens, several mountsEach mount checked separatelySigma's 56mm f/1.4 alone weighs from 256 g to 295 g across its seven mounts.

Weather sealing

A camera or lens is marked sealed only when its maker claims dust, splash or moisture resistance for that product.

  • Maker says nothing: not sealed.
  • Only a rubber gasket at the mount: not sealed.
  • Sealed only with an extra accessory (the X100VI needs an adapter ring and filter): not sealed.
  • A review calling a body "robust": not a claim.

How a check works

  1. For each item, we read the maker's spec and write down, field by field, our stored value, the maker's value and a verdict.
  2. Differences under 1 g or 0.5 mm count as rounding and are left alone.
  3. Before calling a number wrong, we check how similar items are stored. Sometimes it's the rule that differs, not the number.
  4. Clear mismatches with the maker are fixed. New rules are decided by the site owner and added to the log below.
  5. Every item we read gets a source citation, even when nothing changed. A changed value records the old and new number, and why.
  6. Numbers we rejected are recorded too, so the next check doesn't "fix" a right number to a wrong one. Makers' own pages sometimes copy figures from one product to another.
  7. The same lens in two brand files must agree; an automated test enforces it.
  8. Whenever we change a link, every product, image and source link on the site is re-checked.
  9. A decision is reopened if a new maker source contradicts it.

Where we can still go wrong

  • Maker pages disappear. Some older Fujifilm and Olympus cameras no longer have a spec page, so their figures can't be re-checked against the maker until we find a manual or an archived spec sheet.
  • Some makers publish specs only as images, or block automated reading.
  • Not everything is checked yet. A small share of items still await a full check.
  • Prices are list prices (RRP), re-audited periodically, not live deals.

We wrote up what our own checks found in the camera specs we got wrong, and why we publish these rules in small site vs big spec databases. Spotted another one? Please open an issue on the GitHub repository.

DateChange
